title: Assessing Per-Sample Membership Inference Vulnerability without Retraining
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Per-sample vulnerability to membership inference depends jointly on structural error and leverage, not on loss alone, with both worsening attack tradeoffs.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, heatmap then two line plots sharing viridis palette
description: Three side-by-side plots using the viridis colormap. The left panel is a heatmap of the expected generalization gap E[Δℓ_i]. Its x-axis is population leverage h̄_ii (0 to 100) and its y-axis is squared error ε_i² (0 to 200+). White contour lines are labeled 10, 50 and 100, and a colorbar on the right runs from dark purple (0) to yellow (above 200). The gap grows toward the upper right. The middle panel plots the theoretical false negative rate against the false positive rate for the optimal attack, with h̄_ii fixed. It has five curves for ε_i = 0, 0.5, 1, 5 and 10. The right panel has the same axes with ε_i fixed and h̄_ii = 5, 10, 50, 100 and 500. In both line plots a dashed diagonal marks random guessing. Curves bow further toward the origin as ε_i or h̄_ii increases, and the yellow curves hug the axes. The eye goes first to the bright heatmap corner, then to the curves bending away from the diagonal.
caption: Generalization gap and membership inference attack performance for the Gaussian linear regression model. (left) Heatmap of the generalization gap $\mathbb{E}[\Delta\ell_i]$ as a function of $\varepsilon_i^2$ and $\bar{h}_{ii}$, estimated with Monte-Carlo. (middle) Theoretical false negative rate (FNR) $\beta_i$ of the optimal attack on the point $i$ as a function of the false positive rate (FPR) $\alpha_i$, for different values of the structural error $\varepsilon_i$, with $\bar{h}_{ii} = 1$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$. (right) Same as (middle) but with fixed $\varepsilon_i = 1$ and $\bar{h}_{ii}$ varying.
abstract: Recent work in the privacy literature shows that sample-targeted membership inference attacks (MIAs) significantly outperform untargeted approaches by a wide margin. Motivated by this observation, we address the following question: can the privacy vulnerability of individual training points be assessed without training shadow models? We show that per-sample exposure to MIA is governed not only by a point's loss, but also by a data-dependent geometric measure. In the linear setting, we derive a closed-form decomposition of individual black-box MIA vulnerability into a population leverage score and a residual loss term, making explicit how sample-dependent geometry translates into privacy exposure. Since the final layer of most modern architectures is linear, we extend this framework to deep networks and propose a surrogate score operating on last-layer representations that requires only a single trained model and no shadow models. Empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and architectures show that our score outperforms loss and gradient-norm baselines at identifying the highest-risk points under state-of-the-art attacks, providing a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded tool for per-sample privacy risk assessment.
